source.title: Scale Dependent Data Duplication
source.authors: Joshua Kazdan; N. Levi; Rylan Schaeffer; Jessica Chudnovsky; Abhay Puri; Bolei He; M. Donmez; O. Koyejo; David L. Donoho

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices; no material cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss across compute-matched training ladders with different amounts of unique data and reports that finite uniqueness can make larger-run losses depart from naive scaling extrapolations. It also tests a correction for those departures.
record.gate_note: The gradient-alignment measurements and embedding nearest-neighbor collision analyses are not held-out language-model loss results and do not test the listed loss-law versions directly. They are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"]. Figure 6 loss values are not transcribed numerically in the text, so those rows use figure-only values and the paper's qualitative descriptions.
record.test_reason: The study trains compute-matched, Chinchilla-style Qwen ladders (34M–344M) on streams sampled with replacement from finite pools of unique documents (K=10^5–10^8). It compares held-out loss with an approximately-infinite-unique baseline and reports that naive ladder extrapolation fails at larger scale under limited uniqueness. That bears on V2, V5 (repeated data) and V7 (curves bending away from a single power law). Finite K is a data bottleneck, which is outside V1's stated condition, so these rows do not test V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that semantic duplicates act increasingly like exact duplicates as models grow more capable, and that semantic collisions grow faster with corpus size than small-corpus trends predict. Limited uniqueness, simulated with exact repeats in 34M–344M models, causes rising loss penalties at larger scale that break naive ladder extrapolation. A fitted collision-aware plane law, usable with an embedding-estimated effective K, restores accurate loss prediction. That correction is fitted on the same runs and relies on an infinite-data baseline.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce either original scaling-law recipe. It trains compute-matched Qwen-architecture ladders under controlled finite-pool sampling, then models and corrects the resulting loss penalty.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured outcome varies with unique-pool size and model scale; gradient semantic sensitivity also varies with training progress and model scale. The synthetic-corpus nearest-neighbor scaling departure appears an order of magnitude earlier than in the real-text corpus.

fits_no_version.finding: A 3-parameter plane law, Δ(C,K)≈aC^βK^−γ, fits the fractional loss penalty across the ladder with about 0.77% mean relative error (0.90% using an embedding-estimated K). The fit is in-sample and requires the infinite-data baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss penalty from limited (semantic) uniqueness follows a power law in compute and effective pool size.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient alignment of semantic-preserving transformations grows with model capability and training progress.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic duplicates produce increasingly aligned gradients as model capability increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Nearest-neighbour embedding similarity departs from small-N power-law fits at large corpus sizes, earlier for synthetic data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic collision rates in corpora grow faster than small-corpus power laws predict.

record.problems: The authors could not train multi-billion-parameter models and simulate semantic duplication through exact document repeats, so the loss consequences of semantic rather than exact duplicates at large scale remain unverified. They also note that EmbeddingGemma-300m embeddings may not be perfectly isotropic or representative. The primary Figure 6 losses are not stated numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: The infinite-unique baseline ladder's loss-vs-compute power law is not reported numerically or fitted. Parameter and token laws with no bottleneck over several orders of magnitude are not tested.
Extrapolation over orders of magnitude: the ladder spans only about 10x in parameters. Extrapolation accuracy under high-uniqueness training is not quantified.
All; the runs are Chinchilla-optimal by construction and no allocation is fitted.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer. Semantic (non-exact) duplicates are modelled only by exact repeats.
Parameter counting, schedules, fitting methods, and disagreement over the compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Loss-vs-compute curve of the approximately-infinite-unique baseline ladder, the only no-bottleneck condition bearing on V1 and V2.
The 2-parameter ratio-only law (u=1/2, v=0) substantially underpredicts the catastrophic K=10^5 main run.
Fractional loss increase relative to baseline per K (Figure 6 right). The text also states the fitted γ is close to 1.

record.verdict_notes: V1 is removed from R1–R8 because finite K is an explicit data bottleneck, which V1 excludes. Only the K=10^5 rows (R1, R2) carry K-specific evidence in the text; the other per-K rows copy the aggregate description. The scale range is about one order of magnitude in parameters.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests loss scaling over compute under finite-uniqueness conditions, but does not test the general parameter-count and token-count laws across several orders of magnitude with the other factors non-bottlenecking.
The study tests extrapolation under finite-uniqueness constraints and a corrected model; it does not test all small-to-large extrapolations under ordinary high-uniqueness training.
Only repeated-data training is tested through controlled exact repeats. Other modalities and regimes such as fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.

The study tests sensitivity to unique-data availability and documents curve departures, but does not compare parameter-counting choices, training schedules, or alternative fitting methods, nor test disagreement about compute-optimal allocation.

relation.reason: The study directly measures train and validation scaling under controlled data uniqueness against a negligible-repeat baseline.

tranche.reason: Controlled finite-pool experiments identify a condition where naive scaling extrapolation fails and requires a uniqueness-dependent correction.

source_check.notes: Exact repeats are a worst-case proxy for semantic duplication; large-model training on semantic duplicates was not directly validated (Appendix B). The restored correction uses measured same-compute baseline losses and fitted parameters; its fit is not evidence of blind extrapolation orders of magnitude beyond the ladder.

statements.correction: Qwen-architecture ladders: 34M–344M parameters; finite pools sampled with replacement; K=10^5 included; small-model train and validation losses consistent with standard extrapolation; larger-scale loss penalties increase; V2 limits_scope across this ladder.
statements.problem: The Qwen finding and K=10^5 are correct, but the challenges label is too strong for the combined small-to-large condition group: small models follow ordinary extrapolation while larger models depart.
